questions.stem: The Common Programme adopted in September 1949 served as:
options: the armistice agreement that ended the war in Korea
the law that set up the people's communes in the villages
an interim constitution for the new People's Republic
the CCP's first Five-Year Plan for building heavy industry
questions.explanation: The Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference adopted the Common Programme, which set out New Democracy and the structure of government until the 1954 Constitution. The Five-Year Plan began in 1953 and the communes in 1958.

questions.stem: In the first years of the People's Republic, under the policy of New Democracy, the government:
options: banned every private business from the first day of the new state
shared power equally with the Guomindang government on Taiwan
was chosen in contested multi-party national elections in 1949
included minor parties and tolerated private business for a time
questions.explanation: New Democracy united workers, peasants, petty bourgeoisie and national bourgeoisie under CCP leadership, so minor parties held some posts and private firms kept operating into the mid-1950s. Real power stayed with the CCP throughout.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how power worked in the PRC's political system after the 1954 Constitution?
options: Regional military commanders governed their provinces largely independently of Beijing
State bodies such as the National People's Congress existed, but real power lay with CCP leaders
The National People's Congress made policy freely after elections contested openly by rival parties
The Premier answered to an elected opposition that could vote the government out of office
questions.explanation: The Constitution created the National People's Congress and state posts such as Chairman of the PRC, but the Politburo and its Standing Committee decided policy, and party members held the key posts in government and army. The military regions of 1949–54 were brought under central control.

questions.stem: Fanshen, the word Chinese peasants used for land reform, literally means:
options: to rectify
to bloom
to turn over
a great leap
questions.explanation: Fanshen means 'to turn over' or 'turn the body', describing peasants throwing off landlord domination and standing up. William Hinton used it as the title of his account of land reform in one village.

questions.stem: Under the Agrarian Reform Law of 1950, land was redistributed after:
options: the state bought the landlords' estates from them at fair market prices
peasants voted by secret ballot to join large state-run collective farms
landlords agreed to hand over their land in return for party membership
work teams classified every household as landlord, rich, middle or poor peasant
questions.explanation: Party work teams assigned class labels, mobilised poor peasants and confiscated landlords' land, tools and animals for redistribution. No compensation was paid, and collective farming came only from the mid-1950s.

questions.stem: Beyond giving land to the poor, land reform in 1950–52 helped consolidate CCP power mainly by:
options: destroying the landlord class and binding poor peasants to the party
creating large state farms run by advisers from the Soviet Union
restoring the traditional authority of clan elders and temples in the villages
holding village elections in which rival parties won many seats
questions.explanation: Struggle meetings and the confiscation of land broke the landlords who had dominated rural China, often violently, and the peasants who gained land had a stake in the new regime. New village leaders were party activists, replacing the old gentry elite.

questions.stem: William Hinton's Fanshen is an eyewitness account of land reform in Long Bow village, written by an American sympathetic to the revolution. It is most useful to historians as evidence of:
options: the total number of people killed during land reform across China
Mao's private views as recorded in meetings of the Politburo
Guomindang land policy after its government retreated to Taiwan
how land reform was organised and experienced in a single village
questions.explanation: Hinton recorded meetings, class labelling and the experiences of individual villagers, which gives rich detail at the local level. One village cannot show national totals, and his sympathy for the revolution is a perspective to weigh when using the source.

questions.stem: China entered the Korean War in October 1950 when:
options: North Korea asked for help to invade the islands of Japan
the Soviet army withdrew from Manchuria and left it exposed
Guomindang forces landed in Korea to attack the Chinese border
UN forces advanced north towards the Yalu River border
questions.explanation: After UN forces under MacArthur crossed the 38th parallel and approached the Yalu, the Chinese People's Volunteers under Peng Dehuai entered the war. The fighting ended in an armistice in July 1953.

questions.stem: The Korean War helped the CCP consolidate power at home mainly because:
options: the war brought large amounts of American aid to rebuild Chinese industry after 1953
the war let the PLA capture Taiwan while the United States was busy in Korea
the 'Resist America, Aid Korea' campaign rallied patriotism and justified hunting enemies
the war ended in a victory that united all of Korea under the rule of the CCP
questions.explanation: The war fused nationalism with loyalty to the party and accompanied the Campaign to Suppress Counter-revolutionaries. The war ended in stalemate, and the US Seventh Fleet's presence in the Taiwan Strait made an invasion of Taiwan impossible.

questions.stem: Thought Reform in the early 1950s required intellectuals to:
options: sit a revived imperial examination before working in the government
study Marxism in small groups and confess their 'bourgeois' errors
travel abroad to study Western parliaments and bring back reforms
join the Guomindang's youth corps to prove their loyalty to China
questions.explanation: Teachers, writers and scientists took part in study sessions, criticism and self-criticism to remould their thinking along party lines. The aim was ideological conformity, not openness to Western models.

questions.stem: The Three Antis campaign (Sanfan) of 1951–52 targeted:
options: landlords, rich peasants and counter-revolutionaries in villages
rightists, revisionists and capitalist roaders in the party
corruption, waste and bureaucracy among officials and cadres
bribery, tax evasion and fraud by owners of private businesses
questions.explanation: Sanfan was aimed at the party and state's own officials, including former Guomindang officials kept on in their posts. Bribery and tax evasion by business owners were the targets of the Five Antis (Wufan) that followed.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes the Five Antis campaign (Wufan) from the Three Antis campaign (Sanfan)?
options: Wufan was aimed at Red Guard factions, Sanfan at university students
Wufan was aimed at private business owners, Sanfan at officials and cadres
Wufan was aimed at officials and cadres, Sanfan at private business owners
Wufan was aimed at landlords in villages, Sanfan at urban intellectuals
questions.explanation: Wufan (1952) attacked bribery, tax evasion, theft of state property, cheating on government contracts and stealing state economic information, all charges against capitalists. Students often reverse the two; Sanfan came first and targeted the bureaucracy.

questions.stem: The Five Antis campaign strengthened the CCP's position mainly by:
options: allowing businesses to sell their goods freely to Western markets after Korea
uniting business owners with the Red Guards against corrupt party officials
weakening private capitalists and bringing their firms under state influence
returning factories confiscated from the Guomindang to their private owners
questions.explanation: Fines, confessions and denunciations by employees left many businesses financially dependent on the state, preparing the way for their conversion into joint state-private enterprises in 1956. The Red Guards did not exist until 1966.

questions.stem: In 1956 most private firms became 'joint state-private enterprises', in which the former owners:
options: became the elected chairmen of the new people's communes nearby
lost control of their firms but received fixed interest payments
kept full control and paid only a small tax on profits to the state
were sent at once to labour camps and their families disinherited
questions.explanation: The socialist transformation of industry and commerce placed state managers in charge, while owners drew interest on their assessed capital and some stayed on as managers. It completed the end of private capitalism with relatively little violence.

questions.stem: The First Five-Year Plan (1953–57), modelled on the Soviet Union, gave priority to:
options: small backyard furnaces in every rural village
private family farms selling in free markets
heavy industry such as steel, coal and machinery
light consumer goods for export to Western markets
questions.explanation: With Soviet loans, advisers and complete factories, the plan built heavy industry and achieved fast industrial growth. Backyard furnaces belonged to the Great Leap Forward of 1958.

questions.stem: The First Five-Year Plan is usually judged an industrial success. Which problem did it leave that Mao hoped the Great Leap Forward would overcome?
options: Heavy industry had been neglected in favour of making consumer goods
China had relied too little on Soviet experts, loans and technology
Private industry had grown too large for the state to control
Farm output lagged behind industry, so grain supply held back further growth
questions.explanation: Investment went overwhelmingly to industry while agriculture grew slowly, yet grain had to feed the cities and pay for Soviet equipment. Mao sought to develop industry and agriculture together through mass mobilisation rather than slow Soviet-style planning.

questions.stem: The Marriage Law of 1950:
options: banned arranged marriages and concubinage and let women seek divorce
made divorce illegal in order to protect the stability of families
required all marriages to be performed in a Confucian ancestral temple
restored the right of parents to choose their children's partners
questions.explanation: The Marriage Law ended arranged marriage, child betrothal, concubinage and bride prices, and gave women the right to divorce and to own property. Many women used it to escape unhappy marriages in the early 1950s.

questions.stem: Which evidence best shows continuity in many rural women's lives after the 1950 Marriage Law?
options: Many still met family pressure and cadres' resistance when they sought divorce
Women were barred from owning land under the 1950 Agrarian Reform Law
The Marriage Law was repealed within a year after protests by peasants
Women were excluded from joining the Chinese Communist Party until 1976
questions.explanation: Despite the law, local cadres and families often discouraged or blocked divorce, and traditional expectations about women's household work persisted. Women did receive land in their own names under land reform, which marks a change rather than continuity.

questions.stem: The Hundred Flowers Campaign of 1956–57 invited:
options: factory owners to sell their firms to the state
intellectuals to criticise the party and its officials
peasants to merge their cooperatives into giant communes
students to destroy the Four Olds in their cities
questions.explanation: Mao's slogan 'let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools of thought contend' encouraged open criticism, which swelled in May–June 1957. Destroying the Four Olds belonged to the Cultural Revolution.

questions.stem: The Hundred Flowers Campaign was followed from mid-1957 by:
options: the first Red Guard rallies held in Tiananmen Square
Lin Biao's compilation of the Quotations from Chairman Mao
the Anti-Rightist Campaign against many who had spoken out
the armistice that ended the fighting of the Korean War
questions.explanation: Hundreds of thousands were labelled 'rightists', losing jobs and being sent to labour camps; Deng Xiaoping helped run the campaign. Intellectuals learned that criticism was dangerous, which silenced warnings during the Great Leap Forward.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the view that the Hundred Flowers was a genuine invitation that went further than Mao expected?
options: The campaign was organised by Liu Shaoqi while Mao opposed it from the start
Criticism soon questioned the party's right to rule, and Mao reversed course within weeks
Mao had all the leading critics arrested before the campaign was even announced
No intellectuals took part, so the party had to invent the critics' statements
questions.explanation: Criticism grew from complaints about officials to attacks on one-party rule, and in June 1957 the party abruptly launched the Anti-Rightist Campaign. Historians disagree on Mao's intentions; the trap view rests partly on Mao's own later claim to have lured 'snakes out of their holes'.

questions.stem: The Great Leap Forward, launched in 1958, aimed to:
options: overtake Britain in steel output through mass mobilisation
copy the Soviet model of slow, steady, centrally planned growth
restore private farming and free markets in the villages
end China's industrial programme and return to farming
questions.explanation: Mao believed the enthusiasm of the masses could achieve rapid industrial and agricultural growth at the same time, and set a goal of surpassing Britain's output within fifteen years. It was a break from the cautious Soviet model.

questions.stem: The people's communes set up in 1958 were:
options: vast rural units combining farming, local industry, militia and mess halls
small private farms owned by individual families and run for profit
factories in the major cities run by elected councils of their own workers
military academies for training officers of the People's Liberation Army
questions.explanation: Communes merged cooperatives into units of thousands of households, organising labour, industry, schools, militia and communal kitchens. They removed private plots, which weakened peasants' incentives.

questions.stem: During the Great Leap Forward, the backyard furnaces mostly produced:
options: farm machinery that replaced hand labour
coal for the cities' new power stations
poor-quality iron of little use to industry
high-grade steel exported to the Soviet Union
questions.explanation: Peasants melted down pots and tools in small furnaces, producing low-grade pig iron while labour was diverted from the harvest. The campaign wasted resources and helped cause the famine.

questions.stem: Which factor best explains why the famine of the Three Bad Years (1959–61) was so severe?
options: Inflated harvest reports led the state to take grain that peasants needed to survive
Peasants left the communes to farm privately and stopped selling their grain to the state
A Japanese naval blockade stopped all imports of grain into China's ports
Red Guards destroyed the harvest in villages accused of supporting rightists
questions.explanation: Fearing to be labelled rightists, cadres reported impossible harvests, and procurement was set on those figures, leaving villages without food. Weather played a part, but historians agree the policies of the Leap were central; the Red Guards did not appear until 1966.

questions.stem: At the Lushan Conference of 1959, Peng Dehuai:
options: announced that the Cultural Revolution would begin the following year
proposed the Hundred Flowers Campaign to win back the intellectuals
criticised the Leap's excesses in a letter to Mao and was purged
was named Mao's successor and given control of the party's daily work
questions.explanation: Peng, the Minister of Defence, wrote privately to Mao about false reporting and 'petty-bourgeois fanaticism'. Mao denounced him as the head of an anti-party clique, and Lin Biao replaced him as Minister of Defence.

questions.stem: Why is the Lushan Conference seen as a turning point in the Great Leap Forward?
options: Peng's purge silenced critics, so radical policies continued as the famine worsened
Mao admitted his mistakes and handed all economic policy to Peng Dehuai
It ended the Sino-Soviet alliance and brought American food aid to China
It abolished the communes and restored private farming across China
questions.explanation: After Lushan, officials competed to show loyalty with new campaigns against 'right opportunism', so procurement stayed high in 1959–60, the worst years of the famine. The retreat from the Leap came only in 1961–62.

questions.stem: After the Great Leap Forward, Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping helped the economy recover by:
options: sending all urban workers to the countryside to grow more grain
allowing private plots, rural markets and more household-based farming
merging the communes into even larger units and closing all markets
launching a new drive to build backyard furnaces in every county
questions.explanation: In the early 1960s Liu and Deng restored private plots and markets and allowed some households to contract for production; Deng's saying that it did not matter what colour a cat was, so long as it caught mice, summed up this pragmatism. Mao later saw these policies as capitalist.

questions.stem: At the Seven Thousand Cadres Conference in early 1962, Liu Shaoqi's speech was significant because he:
options: suggested the disaster owed more to human error than to natural causes
praised the Great Leap Forward as a complete success for Mao's leadership
called on students to form Red Guard units to defend Mao Zedong Thought
announced that China would go to war with the Soviet Union over the border
questions.explanation: Liu's frank assessment implied criticism of the Leap and of Mao, who made a limited self-criticism and for a time left economic recovery to Liu and Deng. Mao's resentment of Liu helps explain why Liu became the main target of the Cultural Revolution.

questions.stem: Frank Dikötter's Mao's Great Famine argues that the famine of 1959–61 was:
options: mainly the result of Mao's policies, enforced through coercion and violence
caused chiefly by natural disasters beyond the control of the party
the result of Soviet sabotage after Moscow withdrew its advisers
a local problem that Mao corrected as soon as he learned of it
questions.explanation: Dikötter, drawing on provincial party archives, stresses that requisitioning, violence by cadres and Mao's refusal to change course turned crisis into catastrophe. The 'natural disasters' explanation was the official line of the time.

questions.stem: The Socialist Education Movement of 1962–66 aimed to:
options: teach peasants to read through a national literacy drive run by the universities
reopen private schools for the children of the former business owners
train young people for technical jobs in the new Soviet-built factories
revive class struggle and clean up corrupt rural cadres in the 'Four Cleanups'
questions.explanation: After the Leap, Mao insisted 'never forget class struggle', and work teams investigated cadres' accounts, granaries, property and work points. Disagreement with Liu over how to run it fed Mao's suspicion of the party leadership.

questions.stem: The Quotations from Chairman Mao, known as the Little Red Book, was first compiled and distributed by:
options: Deng Xiaoping's party Secretariat
Jiang Qing's Ministry of Culture
Lin Biao's People's Liberation Army
Liu Shaoqi's State Council ministries
questions.explanation: Lin Biao, Minister of Defence from 1959, had the PLA's General Political Department compile the Quotations for soldiers' study, and it became the key text of Mao's cult. This raised Lin's standing as Mao's most loyal follower.

questions.stem: Mao's big-character poster 'Bombard the Headquarters' (August 1966) encouraged:
options: attacks on leaders within the party itself, implicitly Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping
attacks on Guomindang command posts across the Taiwan Strait by the People's Liberation Army
a campaign of bombing raids against American bases in South Vietnam
the destruction of Soviet consulates in Beijing and Shanghai by students
questions.explanation: Mao's poster accused unnamed leading comrades of suppressing the mass movement, signalling that the enemy was inside the party leadership. It opened the way for attacks on Liu and Deng.

questions.stem: Red Guards were told to destroy the 'Four Olds', which were:
options: old landlords, old merchants, old priests and old officials
old temples, old books, old paintings and old furniture
old provinces, old dynasties, old borders and old laws
old customs, old culture, old habits and old ideas
questions.explanation: The campaign against the Four Olds in 1966 led to attacks on temples, books, art and people seen as linked to traditional or foreign culture. The targets were defined as ideas and ways of life, though the attacks fell on objects and people.

questions.stem: During the Cultural Revolution, Liu Shaoqi was:
options: denounced as a 'capitalist roader', expelled from the party, and died in detention
made Mao's official successor and given command of the Red Guard movement
sent to Moscow as ambassador to repair relations with the Soviet leadership
put in charge of the Gang of Four's model operas and cultural policy
questions.explanation: Labelled 'China's Khrushchev', Liu was humiliated at struggle sessions, expelled from the party in 1968 and died in 1969 after being denied proper medical care. It was Lin Biao who was named successor in 1969.

questions.stem: From late 1968, Mao ended the Red Guards' role mainly by:
options: giving the Red Guard leaders seats in the National People's Congress
sending millions of urban youth 'up to the mountains and down to the countryside'
enrolling all Red Guards as officers in the People's Liberation Army reserve
reopening the universities and admitting every Red Guard without any entrance examinations
questions.explanation: After violent factional fighting, workers' teams and the PLA restored order, and the sent-down youth movement moved millions of young people to rural areas. Many lost their education and saw it as a betrayal of their loyalty to Mao.

questions.stem: Jiang Qing's main influence on culture during the Cultural Revolution was:
options: promoting a small set of revolutionary model operas and ballets
restoring traditional Peking opera about emperors, generals and scholars
inviting Western orchestras to perform for the Red Guards
leading the Hundred Flowers debate among China's writers
questions.explanation: As a leader of the Central Cultural Revolution Group, Jiang Qing promoted the 'model works' such as The Red Detachment of Women and Taking Tiger Mountain by Strategy, while most other art was banned. Traditional opera was denounced as feudal.

questions.stem: The Gang of Four, arrested in October 1976 after Mao's death, were:
options: Lin Biao, Chen Boda, Kang Sheng and Ye Qun
Liu Shaoqi, Deng Xiaoping, Peng Zhen and Lu Dingyi
Zhou Enlai, Hua Guofeng, Ye Jianying and Li Xiannian
Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen
questions.explanation: The four radicals, led by Mao's wife Jiang Qing, had driven the later Cultural Revolution and were arrested by Hua Guofeng with military support. Liu, Deng and Peng Zhen were among their victims, not allies.

questions.stem: Which group, although part of the ruling elite, was a main target of Red Guard attacks?
options: Senior PLA commanders loyal to Defence Minister Lin Biao
Leaders of the rebel factions in the Shanghai factories
Party cadres accused of being 'capitalist roaders'
Members of the Central Cultural Revolution Group
questions.explanation: Red Guards and rebels attacked teachers, officials and party secretaries at every level, parading them in dunce caps and forcing confessions. The Central Cultural Revolution Group directed the movement rather than being its target.

questions.stem: Lin Biao, named Mao's successor in 1969, died in a plane crash in Mongolia in 1971 after an alleged plot against Mao. Why did this affair damage the Cultural Revolution?
options: It caused Jiang Qing to resign from the Politburo and leave politics
Mao's chosen successor and chief promoter of his cult was declared a traitor
It ended the Sino-Soviet split and brought Soviet troops back to China
It restored Liu Shaoqi to power and reversed the purges of 1966–68
questions.explanation: If the man who had built Mao's cult and been written into the party constitution as successor was a traitor, Mao's judgement looked flawed, and many people became disillusioned. Liu had died in 1969, and Jiang Qing remained powerful until 1976.

questions.stem: A historian arguing that the PRC under Mao showed continuity with imperial China would most likely point to:
options: the nationalisation of industry and commerce completed in 1956
rule by one supreme leader whose authority was treated as beyond question
the abolition of the landlord class through land reform in the nation's villages
the legal equality given to women by the Marriage Law of 1950
questions.explanation: Mao's cult, his court-like politics and the expectation of loyalty to the ruler are often compared with imperial rule. Land reform, the Marriage Law and nationalisation are examples of change, not continuity.

questions.stem: Which development best shows lasting change in Chinese society between 1912 and 1976?
options: The landlord class that had dominated rural China was destroyed
Power stayed in the hands of a small, unelected political elite
Peasants remained the large majority of the population
Officials continued to be chosen through Confucian examinations
questions.explanation: Land reform eliminated the landlord-gentry class that had controlled villages for centuries. An unelected elite and a peasant majority are continuities, and the Confucian examinations had been abolished in 1905, before this period.

questions.stem: The 'iron rice bowl' in the PRC referred to:
options: a prize for cadres who reported record harvests to Beijing
a slogan of the campaign to build steel furnaces in 1958
guaranteed lifetime jobs and welfare through the work unit
a ration of rice issued daily in the communal mess halls
questions.explanation: Urban workers in state enterprises had secure jobs, housing, health care and pensions through their danwei, or work unit. It was a privilege that rural commune members did not share.
